{{Short description|Formula that calculates option prices for dividend-paying stocks}}
In [[mathematical finance]], '''Margrabe's formula'''<ref>William Margrabe, [http://www.stat.nus.edu.sg/~stalimtw/MFE5010/PDF/margrabe1978.pdf "The Value of an Option to Exchange One Asset for Another"], [[Journal of Finance]], Vol. 33, No. 1, (March 1978), pp. 177-186.</ref> is an [[option (finance)|option]] pricing formula applicable to an option to exchange one risky asset for another risky asset at maturity. It was derived by [[William Margrabe]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20040302080620/finmath.com/Chicago/NAFTCORP/Seminar/BioMargrabe.htm Biography], finmath.com (archived)</ref> in 1978. Margrabe's paper has been cited by over 2000 subsequent articles.<ref>[[Google Scholar]]'s [https://scholar.google.com/scholar?cites=11754033794255374583&as_sdt=2005&sciodt=0,5&hl=en "cites" page for this article]</ref>

==Formula==
Suppose ''S<sub>1</sub>(t)'' and ''S<sub>2</sub>(t)'' are the prices of two risky assets at time ''t'', and that each has a constant continuous dividend yield ''q<sub>i</sub>''. The option, ''C'', that we wish to price gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to exchange the second asset for the first at the time of maturity ''T''. In other words, its payoff, ''C(T)'', is max(0, ''S<sub>1</sub>(T) - S<sub>2</sub>(T))''.

If the volatilities of ''S<sub>i</sub>''{{'s}} are ''&sigma;<sub>i</sub>'', then <math> \textstyle\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2 \sigma_1\sigma_2\rho}</math>, where ''&rho;'' is the Pearson's correlation coefficient of the Brownian motions of the ''S<sub>i</sub>'' 's.

Margrabe's formula states that the fair price for the option at time 0 is:

:<math>e^{-q_1 T}S_1(0) N(d_1) - e^{-q_2 T}S_2(0) N(d_2)</math>

:where:
::<math>q_1,q_2</math> are the expected dividend rates of the prices <math>S_1,S_2</math> under the appropriate risk-neutral measure,
::<math>N</math> denotes the [[cumulative distribution function]] for a [[normal distribution|standard normal]], 
::<math>d_1 = (\ln (S_1(0)/S_2(0)) + (q_2 - q_1 + \sigma^2/2)T)/ \sigma\sqrt{T}</math>, 
::<math>d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}</math>.

==Derivation==
Margrabe's model of the market assumes only the existence of the two risky assets, whose prices, as usual, are assumed to follow a [[geometric Brownian motion]]. The volatilities of these Brownian motions do not need to be constant, but it is important that the volatility of ''S<sub>1</sub>/S<sub>2</sub>'', ''&sigma;'', is constant. In particular, the model does not assume the existence of a riskless asset (such as a [[zero-coupon bond]]) or any kind of [[interest rate]]. The model does not require an equivalent risk-neutral probability measure, but an equivalent measure under S<sub>2</sub>.

The formula is quickly [[Mathematical proof|proven]] by reducing the situation to one where we can apply the [[Black-Scholes formula]].  
*First, consider both assets as priced in units of ''S<sub>2</sub>'' (this is called 'using ''S<sub>2</sub>'' as [[numeraire]]'); this means that a unit of the first asset now is worth ''S<sub>1</sub>/S<sub>2</sub>'' units of the second asset, and a unit of the second asset is worth 1.  
*Under this change of numeraire pricing, the second asset is now a riskless asset and its dividend rate ''q<sub>2</sub>'' is the interest rate. The payoff of the option, repriced under this change of numeraire, is max(0, ''S<sub>1</sub>(T)/S<sub>2</sub>(T) - 1)''.  
*So the original option has become a [[call option]] on the first asset (with its numeraire pricing) with a strike of 1 unit of the riskless asset. Note the dividend rate ''q<sub>1</sub>'' of the first asset remains the same even with change of pricing.
*Applying the [[Black-Scholes formula]] with these values as the appropriate inputs, e.g. initial asset value ''S<sub>1</sub>(0)/S<sub>2</sub>(0)'', interest rate ''q<sub>2</sub>'', volatility ''&sigma;'', etc., gives us the price of the option under numeraire pricing. 
*Since the resulting option price is in units of ''S<sub>2</sub>'', multiplying through by ''S<sub>2</sub>(0)'' will undo our change of numeraire, and give us the price in our original currency, which is the formula above. Alternatively, one can show it by the [[Girsanov theorem]].
